job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Maya Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented room in a flat in Northgate with my friend Priya, so mornings start with a queue for the bathroom. I spend the morning on applications and the early afternoon on a small project, a battery monitor on a breadboard, so I have something to show. I finished electrical engineering six months ago, top of my year, and my final project was a controller for a small solar inverter. I did two internships at the regional power utility, in the substation planning team and on a metering project. My mum is a nurse and sends me articles about jobs, which is sweet and slightly stressful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief, but a muddy one. Friends in software would feel it more than people in electrical work, so I'd tell them to stay calm and keep going. Online I'd say hype cycles hurt graduates because firms freeze hiring first and think later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job market stays slow and I still have to do the hard work of getting in. I've sent about 90 applications and had six interviews, and two reached a final round. My rent share is the thing that keeps me awake, plus a loan of about eleven thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying to utilities, grid contractors and consultancies, and I'd ask Pete, my supervisor at the utility, to introduce me to people. I'd also take a short contract, even a few weeks of site surveying, to keep money coming in. And I'd finish the battery monitor and put it on a portfolio page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady but impatient. It's the not-knowing I can't stand, the open-ended waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms freeze hiring first and think later. Who is responsible for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who set graduate budgets, mostly. They treat us as the cheapest line to cut when they feel nervous. I think there should be rules, like public funding for graduate placements, so the whole market doesn't hold its breath at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a short contract do for you that waiting doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It pays a month of rent and gives me something recent on my CV. Employers look at the last three months and see a gap, even if it's not my fault. Priya got a six-week contract last spring and it led to a real offer.

say: I'd tell friends it's a **relief**, but hiring freezes still hurt graduates most.
I'd say we need public funding for **graduate placements** so firms stop freezing together.
think: The market stays **slow**, so getting in is still on me, and the loan weighs on me.
I'm anxious about **rent**, not about AI, since my own work looks safe.
do: Apply to **utilities and grid contractors**, and ask Pete for introductions.
Take a short **site surveying contract** to keep money coming in.
Finish the **battery monitor** and put it on a portfolio page.
feel: Steady but **impatient**, bothered most by the open-ended waiting.
S0.quote: Employers look at the last three months and see a gap, even if it's not my fault.
fieldNote: Maya's worry is **rent and waiting**, not AI; she wants public support for graduate placements.
She reads recent gaps on a CV as the real **employer** problem.
Practical: contracts, portfolio, introductions from her old supervisor.

steps.text: Apply to grid contractors and utilities and ask Pete to introduce me
Finish the battery monitor and put it on a portfolio page
Take a short site surveying contract to cover a month of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift, but the human parts of engineering are staying. I'd tell friends in software to learn to check what the tools produce. Online I'd back rules that make firms say where AI is used and who is responsible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Design calculations, load studies, paperwork and drawings are exactly what these tools will take on. That is a lot of what juniors do in their first two years. So the entry rung might be thinner, and I'd be applying for fewer of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools properly, not just now and then. I'd learn a power-systems simulation package and show I can use AI to run a load study faster and still catch mistakes. I'd also aim at roles that involve site work, since robots arrive slowly there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and worried at the same time. The tools are interesting, but I can see the junior desk job going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the entry rung might be thinner. How would you cope with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By being the junior who is also useful on site. A firm that sees me running a test at a substation, not just a spreadsheet, can't replace me with software that day. It's the combination that I'd sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Priya in software, because her field is moving fast. And my mum's hospital, which is already cutting admin staff. I'd hate for us all to be fighting for the same shrinking set of roles.

say: I'd say the **human parts** of engineering stay, and firms should say where AI is used.
I'd tell software friends to **check** what the tools produce, not trust it.
think: Design calculations and drawings are what juniors do first, so the **entry rung** may thin out.
The tools are **interesting**, but I can see the junior desk job going.
do: Use AI tools **properly** for load studies and learn a power-systems simulation package.
Aim at **site-based** roles where robots arrive slowly.
Show employers a **portfolio** with tool-assisted work and my own checks.
feel: **Excited and worried** together, curious about the tools but wary for juniors.
S1.quote: A firm that sees me running a test at a substation, not just a spreadsheet, can't replace me with software that day.
fieldNote: Maya adapts: she treats AI as something to **learn** and checks the result herself.
She protects her position by pairing **site work** with desk skills.
Concern extends to **Priya** and her mum's hospital admin staff.

steps.text: Use AI tools on a load study and check every result by hand
Learn a power-systems simulation package through an online course
Apply for graduate roles that include substation and site testing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is scary, and I'd say so. I'd tell friends it's time for public support, retraining money and rules about what firms can replace. I'd say this online too, but calmly, because panic posts don't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my degree loses a lot of value, especially the design side. The hands-on side is safe until about 2031, and I could aim there. But the engineers who sign off big projects will be the ones who already have jobs, and I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job near the grid, even a technician apprenticeship, and stop caring whether it matches my degree. I'd cut spending hard, down to the bare rent and food. I'd also ask my mum if I can move home for a year to save, though I'd hate to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, a bit numb. It feels like I trained for a world that's disappearing as I graduate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take an apprenticeship. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a little proud and a little hurt. I worked for four years and I'd be starting like a school leaver. But a pair of hands at a substation is useful until 2031 at least, and I'd rather be useful than top of a list nobody reads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't worry, and she'd see right through me, because she works nights and knows what exhausted looks like. I'd tell her I have a plan and then I'd make sure it's true.

say: I'd say it's time for **retraining money** and rules on what firms can replace.
I'd keep my online tone **calm**, because panic posts don't help anyone.
think: My degree loses a lot of **value**, especially the design side, and I have no job yet.
The hands-on side holds until about **2031**, so I'll aim there.
do: Take a **technician apprenticeship** near the grid, even if it undersells my degree.
Cut spending to **rent and food** only.
Ask Mum about moving home for a **year** to save.
feel: Scared and a little **numb**, like I trained for a world that's disappearing.
S2.quote: I'd rather be useful than top of a list nobody reads.
fieldNote: Maya accepts a **step down** into an apprenticeship once the clock is two years.
Moves from design to the **hands-on** side that robots reach later.
She protects her mum from worry while quietly making a plan.

steps.text: Apply for technician apprenticeships at the utility and grid contractors
Cut spending to rent, food and the loan payment only
Move back to Mum's for a year to save two thousand
Tell Mum the plan and call her every Sunday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a window, and I'd treat it like one. I'd tell friends to pick a field that's partly hands-on and get qualified now. Online I'd argue for a national retraining fund, funded by the firms that cut people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my chance is to be there when the grid itself has to change. Whatever AI does, the power system needs people who understand it physically. If I get in during the next year, I can build five years of site experience before things settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first sensible job, even at lower pay, and ask to rotate into field work. I'd do an evening course on AI for engineering and a safety certificate. I'd also put a few hundred pounds a month into a savings account so I'm not caught short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously hopeful. It still feels like a fast clock, but I can see a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move from hopeful to worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the utility froze hiring altogether. Or if the loan interest went up while I'm still on trainee pay. Those two together would be the thing, because I couldn't absorb both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from your friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get out onto sites earlier. Most of my course mates want to stay at a screen because it's comfortable. I think comfortable is the riskiest place to be.

say: I'd argue for a **retraining fund** paid by firms that cut staff.
I'd tell friends to get **qualified** in something partly hands-on now.
think: The power system needs people who understand it **physically**, whatever AI does.
If I get in this year I can build **five years** of site experience.
do: Take the first **sensible job** and ask to rotate into field work.
Do an evening course on **AI for engineering** plus a safety certificate.
Save a few hundred a month to avoid being **caught short**.
feel: **Cautiously hopeful**; the clock is fast, but there is a way through.
S3.quote: I think comfortable is the riskiest place to be.
fieldNote: Maya treats five years as a **window** and plans to build site experience inside it.
She sees staying at a screen as **comfortable and risky**.
Her worry list is short: a hiring freeze plus **loan interest**.

steps.text: Accept the first sensible engineering job and ask to rotate into field work
Take an evening course on using AI for engineering design
Get a site safety certificate within six months
Save three hundred a month in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels almost generous. I'd say so, and I'd tell friends not to waste it. Online I'd write something about using the decade to build skills and push for retraining that actually exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine, but only if I use the time well. Ten years means I could do a master's in power systems, or work and study in parallel. By 2036 I'd have six years of experience, which is more than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job within the year, then do a part-time master's in energy systems. I'd rent my own place by 28 and put away something for a deposit. I'd also stay close to the union branch at the utility, because the people there know how change gets managed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, if I'm honest. I'd still check the news every day, but I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd be fine. What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year. I've got no offer yet, and ten years of runway doesn't pay this month's rent. And even a long warning can be wasted if firms and government keep saying later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you rely on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete from the utility for advice, my mum for emergencies, and Priya for company. I'd also trust a union branch more than a company HR team, as it's the group that fights for people on my level.

say: I'd say ten years is **almost generous** and tell friends not to waste it.
I'd push for **retraining** schemes that actually exist, not just promises.
think: I'd be fine if I use the time well, with about **six years** of experience by 2036.
The danger is the **first year**, since a long runway doesn't pay this month's rent.
do: Take a job within the year, then start a part-time **energy systems master's**.
Save for a **deposit** and rent my own place by 28.
Stay close to the **union branch** at the utility.
feel: Pretty **calm**; I'd still read the news daily, but I'd sleep.
S4.quote: Ten years of runway doesn't pay this month's rent.
fieldNote: Maya's calm depends on landing a **first job**, which she says plainly.
She trusts **union** and mentor advice over HR departments.
Ten years lets her plan study and a deposit rather than just survive.

steps.text: Land an engineering job within the year and stay in it
Start a part-time master's in energy systems
Save for a flat deposit and rent my own place by 28
Join the union branch at the utility

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be twenty-five with a degree that's lost its edge and a loan. What would help is retraining money, a real apprenticeship route into the grid, and rules that make firms keep taking on graduates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not as sure of myself as I sound. I like using the tools now and then, but I keep wondering if I'm using the tools to help myself or to help someone replace me. That question doesn't go away.

headlineQuote: I keep wondering if I'm using the tools to help myself or to help someone replace me.
portrait: Maya is a 23-year-old **electrical engineering** graduate, top of her year, sharing a rented room in Northgate with her friend Priya.
She has had about 90 applications and six interviews, and carries an **eleven thousand** loan with a short cushion.
She leans left, wants public funding for **graduate placements** and trusts union branches over company HR.
She is steady with technology: she uses AI **now and then** and moves toward site work, which robots reach later.
Her mood tracks rent and the first job, not fear of AI; it spikes in **two years** and eases with time.
biggestWorry: The two-year **AGI** picture worries her most, with her degree losing edge while she carries a loan.
whatWouldHelp: She would want retraining money, a real **apprenticeship** route into the grid, and rules making firms keep hiring graduates.
